world.title: The Baltic states fear a Russian invasion. They faced the same threat a century ago and failed to stop it. Historian Alexey Uvarov explains why the region could not defend itself against Stalin. — Med
world.description: As Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine enters its fifth year, experts and Western intelligence sources are increasingly warning that Russia also poses a growing threat to countries in the Baltic region. So far, the confrontation has produced only isolated incidents, such as drone incursions into these countries’ territory — but tensions are rising. Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Poland, and Finland increasingly need to consider how they would collectively defend themselves against a full-scale invasion from the east. The problem is not new to the region: 100 years ago, the Baltic countries also tried to join forces to protect themselves from militarily stronger neighbors. They failed to create an effective defense alliance. In this article for Meduza, historian and memory-politics expert Alexey Uvarov examines lessons from the Baltic region’s failed efforts to build an effective defense alliance.

science.title: Citizen science reveals patterns of distributional decline and expansion across 1864 native vascular plant species in Kanagawa, Japan
science.description: Rapid land-use change and climate change increase the need for quantitative, region-wide assessments of current status across many plant species. Long-term citizen-led distribution surveys help meet this need, and European examples in particular have been widely recognized internationally. In contrast, comparable efforts in non-English-speaking regions remain underrepresented due to language barriers. We present a citizen-science project in Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan, and analyze presence–absence data from three distribution surveys (1979–1987, 1996–2000, 2013–2017) conducted under this project to quantify changes in the number of presence-recorded survey districts for 1864 native vascular plant species. Presence-recorded districts decreased for 835 species (44.8%), especially grassland, forest-edge, upland field, and wasteland species. By contrast, 688 species (36.9%) increased, particularly evergreen forest species. Within this group, mycoheterotrophic orchids and ferns typical of dark, humid understories expanded rapidly, suggesting effects of coppice-forest abandonment. Although the annual disappearance rate of presence-recorded districts declined over 1979–2017, the recent disappearance rate remained significantly greater than zero, indicating ongoing habitat loss. Using disappearance rates, we identified 53 non-threatened species with disappearance rates comparable to or exceeding those of threatened species, and define them as “potentially threatened species.” These results underscore the value of long-term, systematic, citizen-led surveys for evidence-based conservation planning. A long-term citizen science project in Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan, reveals that from 1979 to 2017, distribution ranges contracted in 44.8% and expanded in 36.9% of all 1,864 native vascular plant species occurring in the prefecture.
